slides.title: Use the bytes you bring close
keyPoints: Spatial locality reuses nearby bytes
Temporal locality reuses a value soon
Reuse competes with other accesses and capacity
slides.narration: A cache commonly brings in a whole line even when a program asks for one small value. Spatial locality means nearby bytes are likely to be useful too. Temporal locality means a recently used value will be needed again before competing work pushes it away. These ideas explain why layout and order matter without requiring a particular cache size. Reuse after a million unrelated accesses may be too late, even if it occurs quickly in clock time. We will count useful bytes and distinct model lines, then verify that two real traversals compute the same answer. Neither step alone is a hardware timing measurement.

question.prompt: Why is nearby storage not automatically useful spatial locality?
question.answer: The program must actually use the nearby bytes before they are displaced; unused neighboring fields still consume transferred space.

slides.title: Translate a stride into bytes before counting lines
keyPoints: Eight four-byte values are used
Stride one touches two sixteen-byte model lines
Stride four touches eight model lines
slides.narration: The model reads eight logical values, each four bytes. With a stride of one element, the selected byte addresses run from zero through twenty-eight, touching two sixteen-byte lines. With stride four, the addresses are sixteen bytes apart, so every value touches a new line: eight lines for the same thirty-two useful bytes. The printed fetched counts are thirty-two and one hundred twenty-eight under this cold unique-line traffic model. They are not observed cache misses or hardware bytes transferred. The example demonstrates why the unit elements is incomplete until element size and line size are supplied.

slides.title: A working set belongs to a phase
keyPoints: Count what must be useful together
Include metadata and code when relevant
Dataset size alone can overstate or understate pressure
slides.narration: A program may own a large dataset while using only one tile at a time. Its active working set during that tile can be small. Conversely, an index, pointer graph, code, and thread stacks may add substantial pressure beyond the obvious input array. Choose an interval such as one request, one loop, or one batch, then ask which values are reused within it. This makes working-set reasoning useful for maintenance: adding a small lookup structure to every record may expand the hot footprint enough to change behavior. Total allocated bytes and useful hot bytes answer related but different questions.

question.prompt: Why is counting only the input array sometimes an underestimate of the working set?
question.answer: Traversal may also repeatedly use indexes, metadata, instructions, stacks, and other state during the same phase.

slides.title: Equal results do not prove equal locality
keyPoints: Both traversals sum the same twelve integer values
Only their visit order differs
Correctness is checked before performance is claimed
slides.narration: This program stores zero through eleven in a flat array representing three rows of four columns. The row-first traversal visits adjacent elements in its inner loop. The column-first traversal jumps by four elements in its inner loop. Both print sixty-six and the equality check prints true because all twelve small integers are added exactly once. That result verifies the intended computation, not a speed difference. A timing claim would need a larger controlled workload, an observed compiler configuration, and a measurement method. The source’s one-line cache model explains a possible consequence of order; this program keeps the real computation contract visible.

slides.title: Chapter 28 — Locality
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Locality is a pattern of reuse.
Temporal locality concerns returning to the same information, while spatial locality concerns accessing nearby information.
Hardware caches and software buffers exploit these patterns by retaining recently useful data and moving adjacent bytes together.
Locality is not a property of a data structure in isolation.

slides.title: Temporal locality
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Temporal locality occurs when an item used now is likely to be used again soon.
A loop repeatedly updating a small set of accumulators exhibits it.
Retaining those values in registers or cache avoids repeated access to slower levels.
“Soon” must be interpreted relative to competing accesses and capacity.
slides.narration: Temporal locality occurs when an item used now is likely to be used again soon. A loop repeatedly updating a small set of accumulators exhibits it. Retaining those values in registers or cache avoids repeated access to slower levels. “Soon” must be interpreted relative to competing accesses and capacity. Reusing an item after touching millions of unrelated bytes may be too late for a small cache. Reuse distance—the intervening distinct data relevant to a cache model—is often more informative than elapsed time alone.

slides.title: Spatial locality
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes.
A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line.
Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction.
Spatial proximity is not automatically useful.
slides.narration: Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes. A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line. Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction. Spatial proximity is not automatically useful. A structure containing many rarely used fields can force frequently used fields to share lines with irrelevant data. A layout that groups the fields used together may reduce transferred bytes without changing the logical records.

SOURCE TOPIC
Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes.
A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line.
Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction.
Spatial proximity is not automatically useful.

blocks.title: Full professor transcript for this slide
blocks.text:
LECTURE NARRATION
Spatial locality occurs when an access predicts accesses to nearby bytes. A sequential array traversal typically uses several elements from each fetched cache line. Fetching an entire line is valuable when the remaining bytes are consumed before eviction. Spatial proximity is not automatically useful. A structure containing many rarely used fields can force frequently used fields to share lines with irrelevant data. A layout that groups the fields used together may reduce transferred bytes without changing the logical records.

slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: A working set is the collection of data and instructions actively used during a relevant phase or interval.
Its size and access order determine pressure on caches, TLBs, and physical memory.
Different phases of one program can have different working sets.
A useful analysis chooses a time scale: one inner loop, one request, one batch, or a steady-state interval.

slides.title: Sequential access
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Sequential access follows adjacent locations in a predictable order.
It can use most bytes of each cache line and allow hardware prefetching to anticipate future accesses.
It also often reduces translation pressure by consuming many bytes within each page.
The benefit depends on actual use.
slides.narration: Sequential access follows adjacent locations in a predictable order. It can use most bytes of each cache line and allow hardware prefetching to anticipate future accesses. It also often reduces translation pressure by consuming many bytes within each page. The benefit depends on actual use. Reading a large array once still incurs compulsory traffic. Sequential order makes that traffic efficient; it does not make the bytes free. Streaming too much unrelated data can also evict useful cached state.

slides.title: Strided access
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Strided access advances by a fixed distance between elements.
Small strides may retain useful spatial locality; large strides may touch a new line or page for every item.
Particular stride patterns can also interact poorly with cache-set indexing.
When analyzing a stride, express it in bytes.
slides.narration: Strided access advances by a fixed distance between elements. Small strides may retain useful spatial locality; large strides may touch a new line or page for every item. Particular stride patterns can also interact poorly with cache-set indexing. When analyzing a stride, express it in bytes. A stride of 16 elements means 64 bytes for four-byte elements but 128 bytes for eight-byte elements. Element count without element size does not determine cache-line use.

slides.title: Random access
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Random access uses an order that is difficult to predict from recent addresses.
It can reduce prefetch usefulness and increase the number of distinct lines or pages needed for a small amount of useful data.
Randomness should be defined carefully: a random permutation of a compact array differs from pointers distributed across a much larger heap.
A benchmark should generate its access order outside the timed region when the goal is to measure memory traversal rather than random-number generation.

It can reduce prefetch usefulness and increase the number of distinct lines or pages needed for a small amount of useful data. Randomness should be defined carefully: a random permutation of a compact array differs from pointers distributed across a much larger heap. A benchmark should generate its access order outside the timed region when the goal is to measure memory traversal rather than random-number generation. It should also preserve dependencies intentionally: independent random loads and dependent pointer chasing test different limits.

slides.title: Row-major versus column-major traversal
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: Assume a row-major 64 × 64 matrix of eight-byte elements and 64-byte cache lines.
A row contains 512 bytes, or eight lines.
Traversing a row consecutively uses eight elements from each line before moving on.
A column traversal advances by 512 bytes between successive elements.
slides.narration: Assume a row-major 64 × 64 matrix of eight-byte elements and 64-byte cache lines. A row contains 512 bytes, or eight lines. Traversing a row consecutively uses eight elements from each line before moving on. A column traversal advances by 512 bytes between successive elements. It touches one element in each of 64 different rows before returning to the next element of the first row. If the relevant cache cannot retain those lines, much of each fetched line is wasted before reuse. If it can retain them, the difference may be smaller. Capacity and associativity determine the result; “column traversal always misses” is too strong. A blocked traversal processes a smaller rectangle before moving elsewhere. For example, an 8 × 8 tile contains 512 bytes of element data. In a transpose or matrix operation, choosing tiles whose active input and output regions fit the useful cache budget can preserve reuse. Include all simultaneously active arrays and temporary storage when estimating the budget.

slides.title: Stride and cache lines
slides.eyebrow: SOURCE CONCEPT · REASON THROUGH THE MECHANISM
keyPoints: For 64-byte cache lines and 8-byte elements, sequentially reading doubles uses eight neighboring elements per fetched line.
Reading every eighth double touches one element per line.
Reading every sixteenth skips a full line between accesses.
Larger strides therefore waste more fetched bytes and reduce spatial locality.
slides.narration:
For 64-byte cache lines and 8-byte elements, sequentially reading doubles uses eight neighboring elements per fetched line. Reading every eighth double touches one element per line. Reading every sixteenth skips a full line between accesses. Larger strides therefore waste more fetched bytes and reduce spatial locality.

In plain English: A cache is like keeping the things you use most often on your desk instead of walking to a storage room every time.

slides.title: Row-major is a layout fact, not a loop-name preference
keyPoints: Flat index = row × column count + column
Adjacent columns are contiguous in this representation
Choose loop order from actual storage layout
slides.narration: In our flat three-by-four array, row one begins at element four because each earlier row contains four elements. Incrementing the column then advances one element at a time. Incrementing the row while holding column fixed advances four elements. That arithmetic, not the names row and column, explains the locality difference. A column-major representation would favor a different order, and a vector of separately allocated rows has additional layout details. Before rewriting loops, verify the actual representation and dependencies. A visually familiar matrix expression is not enough to prove which objects sit next to each other in memory.

question.answer: No. The access order should follow the actual contiguous dimension and the computation’s dependency requirements.

slides.title: Packing hot fields can reduce unused traffic
keyPoints: Records may contain rarely used fields
A hot pass may need only one small field
Layout changes trade locality against interface complexity
slides.narration: Suppose each record occupies sixty-four bytes, but a repeated analysis reads only a four-byte score. A record-at-a-time layout may fetch many unused bytes with each score. A separate compact score array can place sixteen scores in the space formerly occupied by one whole record. This is a potential traffic improvement, not an automatic recommendation: other operations may need complete records, and keeping parallel arrays synchronized adds maintenance obligations. Identify which phase dominates and preserve the correspondence between fields. A locality change is worthwhile when it improves the measured workload without making the data model unreliable.
actions: Ask for a concrete access sequence and calculation before opening the answer.

question.prompt: What correctness invariant becomes important when one record structure is split into parallel arrays?
question.answer: Entries at the same logical index must continue to describe the same record, including during insertion and removal.

slides.title: Randomness and dependence are separate properties
keyPoints: A random permutation may still fit in cache
Pointer chasing hides the next address until a load completes
Generate unrelated random choices outside a traversal measurement
slides.narration: Calling a benchmark random does not describe its whole memory behavior. A shuffled order over a compact array may reuse a small number of pages, while pointers scattered across a large heap may touch many. Independent random loads can overlap; a dependent linked chain may wait for each previous result. Generating random numbers inside the timed region adds another workload entirely. Define the distribution, size, dependency pattern, and setup boundary before interpreting a result. Otherwise a supposed memory test may mostly measure random-number generation or a different working set from the real application.

question.prompt: Why should a traversal benchmark usually prepare its random order before timing?
question.answer: So the measured region reflects traversal rather than also paying for random-order generation, unless that generation is intentionally part of the task.

slides.title: The one-resident-line model has a narrow claim
keyPoints: The source model keeps only one line
It isolates reuse order in a tiny matrix
It does not predict a modern cache’s exact miss count
slides.narration: The chapter’s compact model reports four misses for row-first traversal and sixteen for column-first traversal of its four-by-four example. Those counts follow its one-resident-line rule. A real cache has more entries, associativity, replacement behavior, and often prefetching, so the same tiny matrix may fit entirely after initial loading. The model remains useful because it shows how visit order changes reuse opportunities under a stated capacity. Do not repeat its numbers as measured performance. When changing the model, record line size, capacity, starting state, and access order together so the reason for a changed count stays visible.

keyPoints: Check values before measuring speed

Changing arithmetic order can change numeric results
slides.narration: Reordering independent additions over our small integers preserves sixty-six. That does not mean every loop can be rearranged freely. A loop may depend on a value updated in the previous iteration, or floating-point rounding may make different summation orders produce different results. A cache-friendly rewrite must preserve the required computational contract, not just the set of addresses touched. Start with correctness checks, then measure the effect under a controlled workload. If the application permits a different numeric approximation, state that as a changed requirement. Otherwise an apparently faster result may simply be doing a different job.
